# Capstone: Secondary Structure Prediction Project {.unnumbered}

## Framing

This project is not a new topic. It's the same problem posed
descriptively on Day 7, using the tools built up from Day 5 (profiles)
through Day 12 (attention): design, train, and evaluate your own
secondary-structure predictor. There is no single correct architecture —
part of the assignment is deciding how to build the model yourself,
informed by what the course covered (a linear/profile score → a
perceptron → a hidden layer → a proper PyTorch model → convolutions →
recurrence → attention) and by your own reading of the literature.

## The task

You are given real protein data and asked to predict, for every residue,
one of three secondary-structure classes: **H** (helix), **E** (strand),
or **C** (coil) — exactly the three-class problem Day 6 and Day 9
introduced with Rost & Sander's PHD method as the historical example.
Your model should be able to use **both** of the input representations
provided (raw sequence and PSSM profile) — comparing what each one buys
you is itself a natural thing to report on.

### Training data

A real, verified dataset of 1,200 protein domains, provided as three
parallel folders sharing the same base filename per entry:

```
dataset/
├── fasta/   # 1,200 files — plain amino-acid sequence, FASTA format
├── dssp/    # 1,200 files — per-residue H/E/C label string (DSSP-derived)
└── pssm/    # 1,200 files — CSV, one row per residue, one column per
             # amino acid (order: A,R,N,D,C,Q,E,G,H,I,L,K,M,F,P,S,T,W,Y,V),
             # values are the position-specific scoring matrix's
             # weighted observed percentages
```

Example entry (`d1g2ra_`): a 96-residue domain, its FASTA sequence, a
DSSP label string of matching length (`CCCCCC...HHHHHHHHHH...`), and a
96-row × 20-column PSSM CSV — all three files verified to correspond to
the same protein.

**[Download the dataset](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1gnxfXXYysCk4L4FYztzeejPVXJaMnxQw?usp=sharing)**
(Google Drive — `dataset.zip`, ~3 MB, 1,200 entries × 3 formats).

## Deliverables

1. **A public Colab notebook** containing the code that produces your
   results — reproducibility (does it actually rerun and reproduce your
   numbers, with a fixed random seed) is graded explicitly.
2. **A short written report as a single PDF**, structured as a research
   paper: introduction, materials/methods, results, conclusion/discussion,
   supplementary material if needed. **Maximum 1000 words** (including
   supplementary). The results section must include:
   - Your predictor's performance (accuracy, MCC, and similar metrics —
     the same evaluation toolkit Day 8 introduced), with training and
     validation loss curves.
   - At least one **ablation study** — how performance changes when you
     vary something about the model (regularization, dropout, which
     input features you use, number of layers, ...).
3. **A code presentation** (~15 minutes: 10 minutes presenting your
   model architecture and training procedure, 5 minutes of questions),
   focused on the deep-learning part of your work, not slides about the
   biology.

This is not an exam — look up papers, discuss with peers, revisit
earlier labs and notes. Just don't plagiarize; reports are checked with
plagiarism software.

## Grading

**Report — 50%:**

| Criterion | Weight | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Format and coherence | 10% | Clear intro/methods/results/discussion structure; stays within 1000 words |
| Answered all required elements | 30% | Every point above is addressed, with figures *and* accompanying written explanation |
| Critical thinking / discussion | 30% | Reasoning about your results, whatever they turned out to be — a honest, well-argued negative result can score well here |
| Figures | 15% | Legible, referenced in the main text (no stand-alone figures), captions written as complete, self-contained sentences |
| Overall impression | 15% | Understanding of the assignment and effort put in; answering beyond the minimum can help here |

**Code presentation — 50%:**

| Criterion | Weight | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Reproducibility | 30% | We rerun your notebook and get your reported numbers back — fix your random seeds |
| Documentation | 20% | Comments throughout, functions/methods explained |
| Explanation of the code | 50% | You walk through your own code live and answer follow-up questions about it — tests understanding, not just working code |
